There are roughly two ways to make an agent better. You can improve the model —
pretraining, RL, post-training of every flavor — or you can improve the
*program* wrapped around it: the prompts, the workflow, the tools, the
scaffold. Call them parameter space and program space. Parameter space is where
the headline gains come from, but it is closed territory: a point of lift costs
a training run, and a handful of labs can pay. Program space is the opposite —
open to anyone, priced in tens of dollars, iterable in an afternoon — and the
same model routinely swings by double digits depending on the harness it runs
inside.<!-- TODO: pin a real number here — SWE-bench leaderboard spread for a
fixed model across scaffolds is the obvious citation -->

![The two axes. Progress so far has climbed the parameter wall — a training
run per step, flattening returns. The program-space direction is open, cheap,
and — as of roughly now — searchable by machine. The gate is model capability:
run the same harness search from a weaker model (gray) and there is little to
gain.](figures/two_axes.png){#fig-two-axes width=88%}

Until recently, program space was searched by hand, which is to say barely:
harness design is a high-dimensional, gradient-free search problem, and humans
explore it by folklore. What changed is that frontier models became good enough
to do the searching — to read an agent's trajectory, diagnose the failure, and
propose an edit. A field has formed around this almost overnight: prompt
evolvers like GEPA [@gepa], workflow searchers like AFlow [@aflow], and the
recursive-self-improvement line — ADAS, the Darwin Gödel Machine — where the
agent rewrites its own scaffold. A new optimizer every few weeks. And if your
instinct is that the next model release makes all of this moot — note that the
argument cuts the other way. The optimizer is a model too. Every release
upgrades the thing that improves the agent, not just the agent.

It is not hard to see where this goes. If program-space search keeps
compounding with model capability, harness design stops being artisanal:
you don't hand-write a scaffold any more than you hand-tune weights — you pick
an optimizer, point it at your agent, and pay for the lift. Agent optimization
becomes a component you choose the way you choose Adam over SGD. For that
future to arrive, one question has to have a measurable answer: *which of these
methods actually works, on what, and at what cost?*

Right now it doesn't. Every optimizer paper grades its own homework: its own
tasks, its own seed agents, its own budget, its own base model — and, when
baselines appear at all, its own reimplementation of the competition. The
numbers never meet. A field that cannot compare its methods cannot tell whether
it is making progress.

![What comparison under one protocol looks like — an early sweep of thirteen
optimizers on BBH-hard, same seed agent, same budget meter. Ranks reorder as
budget grows; a leaderboard is just the right-hand edge of this
plot.](figures/anytime_curve_bbh_named.png){#fig-anytime-bbh width=100%}

MABench is our attempt at the measuring stick. It runs agent-optimization
methods — vendored verbatim, never reimplemented — against the same seed
agents, on the same task suites, under the same metered budget, with test
scores sealed until the run is over. The method is the only variable. The
deliverable is not a leaderboard number but an anytime curve — how much lift
over the seed agent a method buys per dollar spent — reported across a grid of
tasks, seeds, and budgets. This post explains the protocol: what a run is, what
gets measured, and why we made the design choices we did. Part 2 reports what
happened when we ran it.

## Anatomy of a run

A run hands the method three things: a copy of the seed agent, a workspace,
and a budget. Inside the workspace it can do whatever it likes — rewrite the
agent's prompt, restructure its workflow, edit its source, spawn its own LLM
calls to think with. We deliberately impose no structure on the search loop.
The method owns its loop; the framework owns everything that has to be
common for the comparison to mean anything: identity, scoring, budget, and
metering.

All of that passes through four endpoints, and the design is in what each one
is allowed to reveal — a disclosure ladder:

| Endpoint | What it does | What the method sees |
|---|---|---|
| `run_train` | run a candidate on training tasks | everything: per-task verdicts (gold included) and, on request, the worker's trajectory |
| `score_dev` | score a candidate on the dev split | a scalar, nothing else — and the check is charged to the method's own budget |
| `score_test` | score a candidate on the held-out test split | nothing — framework-only, sealed until the run ends |
| `spend` | query the meter | its own ledger — free, so budget discipline is expressible |

The ladder exists because optimizers differ in what feedback they can even
consume. A prompt hill-climber needs only the `score_dev` scalar; GEPA's whole
mechanism is *reading* the training trajectories and reflecting on the
failures. So training feedback comes in two facets — the dataset's verdict on
each task, and the worker's trajectory getting there — while dev feedback
is deliberately starved down to a number that costs budget to look at, and
test feedback doesn't exist at all. A method cannot overfit what it never
sees.

Two more pieces of bookkeeping do most of the benchmark's work. First, the
**stamp**: whenever the method believes it has a new best candidate, it says
so. Each stamp is recorded with the spend at that moment, and the stamped
candidates are scored — later, by us, on the sealed test split. The sequence
of (spend, test score) points *is* the anytime curve; the method never grades
itself. Second, the **per-actor ledger**: every token in the run is metered
and attributed either to the meta-agent (the optimizer thinking) or to the
workers (the agent doing tasks). The split matters — two methods with the same
total spend can be doing completely different things with it, and Part 2 shows
exactly that.

When the budget runs out, the run is over. What survives is everything the
comparison needs and nothing the method can spin: the stamped candidates, the
curve, the ledger, and a trace of every call the method made along the way.
